questions.question: At equilibrium the concentrations stop changing. Does the reaction stop? Explain with rates.
questions.solution: No — forward and reverse reactions continue at EQUAL rates: every product formed is consumed at the same rate, so concentrations are constant, not zero-change. Equilibrium is dynamic balance, not standstill. Isotopic labelling experiments prove the exchange continues.

questions.question: Why do changes in concentration, pressure or catalyst fail to change the equilibrium constant K?
questions.solution: K = ratio of rate constants (k_f/k_r), and rate constants depend only on TEMPERATURE (and catalyst equally on both sides, cancelling). Concentration/pressure changes shift the POSITION (amounts at equilibrium) but not the ratio that defines K. Only temperature alters the rate constants themselves.

questions.concept: Le Chatelier applied to Haber process
questions.question: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ. Predict the effect of (a) raising pressure, (b) raising temperature, (c) removing NH₃ — with reasons.
questions.solution: (a) Higher pressure shifts toward fewer gas moles (4 → 2): more NH₃. (b) Exothermic forward reaction — higher T shifts BACKWARD (toward endothermic direction), lowering yield; that is why Haber runs at moderate ~450 °C with a catalyst for speed. (c) Removing NH₃ makes Q < K, so the system replaces it — forward shift, higher conversion. Each prediction is the system opposing the imposed change.

questions.question: What does it mean when the reaction quotient Q is less than, equal to, or greater than K?
questions.solution: Q < K: too few products — the reaction proceeds FORWARD until Q = K. Q = K: at equilibrium, no net change. Q > K: too many products — the reaction runs BACKWARD. Q is the same expression as K but evaluated at the CURRENT composition; comparing them predicts the direction at any instant.

questions.question: Why does adding a catalyst speed up a reaction but leave the equilibrium composition unchanged?
questions.solution: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of BOTH forward and reverse reactions equally — k_f and k_r multiply by the same factor, so their ratio K is unchanged. Equilibrium is reached FASTER, but the position is thermodynamics, not kinetics. The catalyst changes the road, not the destination.

questions.question: A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions. Why does it leave the equilibrium position unchanged?
questions.solution: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of BOTH directions by the same amount, so both rates increase by the same factor. The point where the two rates become equal — equilibrium — therefore stays at the same composition. Catalysts change how fast equilibrium arrives, never where it sits.

questions.concept: Why K changes only with temperature
questions.question: Changing pressure or concentration shifts an equilibrium, yet K stays constant. Why is temperature the only variable that changes K?
questions.solution: K is defined from the standard free-energy change, and ΔG° depends only on temperature: ln K = −ΔG°/RT. Pressure and concentration changes just move the system along the same equilibrium surface (Q ≠ K temporarily, then Q → K again). Temperature alters ΔG° itself, so it resets K. Pressure changes position; temperature changes the destination.

questions.concept: Why Le Chatelier's principle is a consequence
questions.question: Why does a system at equilibrium respond to an added reactant by making more product?
questions.solution: Adding reactant makes the reaction quotient Q fall below K. The system is no longer at equilibrium, and the only way to restore Q = K is to consume some of the added reactant — i.e. the forward reaction runs faster until Q returns to K. Le Chatelier's principle is a shorthand for this Q-versus-K restoration, not an independent law.
